Remember that the absolute value function can be defined in two different ways. First, we can define it as the following piecewise function:

sections.normalized_html:
First, recall that [MATH: \sqrt{x^2} = |x|.] Therefore, we can rewrite the limit as

[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to 0^-} \dfrac{|x|}{x}.]

Let's attempt to evaluate this limit by direct substitution. Substituting [MATH: x=0] into the limit, we obtain

[MATH: lim_(x → 0^{−})(|x|)/(x)|= (|0|)/(0) = (0)/(0)]

which is an indeterminate form.

Notice, however, that we only require the left-sided limit, i.e., [MATH: x\to0^{-}.] If [MATH: x < 0,] then [MATH: |x| = -x.] Therefore, we can evaluate this limit as follows:

[MATH: lim_(x → 0^{−})((|x|)/(x))|= lim_(x → 0^{−})((− x)/(x)); = lim_(x → 0^{−})((− x)/(x)); = lim_(x → 0^{−})(− 1); = − 1]

Finally, we conclude that

[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to 0^-} \dfrac{\sqrt{x^2}}{x} = -1.]

items.title: Evaluating a Limit Containing a Radical and an Absolute Value Function

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's attempt to evaluate this limit by direct substitution. Substituting [MATH: x=1] into the limit, we obtain

[MATH: lim_(x → 1^{+})(|x − 1|)/(sqrt(x − 1))|= (|1 − 1|)/(sqrt(1 − 1)); = (|0|)/(0); = (0)/(0)]

which is an indeterminate form.

Notice, however, that we only require the right-sided limit, i.e., [MATH: x\to1^{+}.] If [MATH: x > 1,] then [MATH: |x-1| = x-1.] Therefore, we can write this limit as follows:

[MATH: lim_(x → 1^{+})(|x − 1|)/(sqrt(x − 1))|= lim_(x → 1^{+})(x − 1)/(sqrt(x − 1))]

Direct substitution into the above still gives an indeterminate form [MATH: \dfrac 0 0.] However, we can rationalize the expression and then evaluate the limit, as follows:

[MATH: lim_(x → 1^{+})(x − 1)/(sqrt(x − 1))|= lim_(x → 1^{+})(x − 1)/(sqrt(x − 1)) ⋅ (sqrt(x − 1))/(sqrt(x − 1)); = lim_(x → 1^{+})((x − 1)sqrt(x − 1))/(x − 1); = lim_(x → 1^{+})((x − 1)sqrt(x − 1))/(x − 1); = lim_(x → 1^{+})(sqrt(x − 1))/(1); = lim_(x → 1^{+})sqrt(x − 1); = sqrt(1 − 1); = sqrt(0); = 0]

items.title: Evaluating a Limit Containing a Quadratic Absolute Value Function

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's attempt to evaluate this limit by direct substitution. Substituting [MATH: x=2] into the limit, we obtain

[MATH: lim_(x → 2^{−})(|x^{2} − 4|)/(x − 2)|= (|2^{2} − 4|)/(2 − 2); = (|4 − 4|)/(2 − 2); = (0)/(0)]

which is an indeterminate form.

To evaluate the limit, we factor the numerator and rewrite the limit, as follows:

[MATH: \eqalign{ \lim_{x \to 2^-} \dfrac {\vert x^2 - 4 \vert} {x - 2} &=\lim_{x \to 2^-} \dfrac {\vert (x+2)(x-2) \vert} {x - 2}\[5pt] &=\lim_{x \to 2^-} \dfrac {\vert x+2\vert \cdot \vert x-2 \vert} {x - 2}\[5pt] }]

Now, since [MATH: x<2,] we have

  • [MATH: |x+2| = x+2] and

  • [MATH: |x-2| = -(x-2).]

Substituting the above into our limit and simplifying, we get

[MATH: lim_(x → 2^{−})(|x + 2|⋅|x − 2|)/(x − 2)|= lim_(x → 2^{−})(− (x + 2)(x − 2))/(x − 2); = lim_(x → 2^{−})(− (x + 2)(x − 2))/(x − 2); = lim_(x → 2^{−}) − (x + 2); = − (2 + 2); = − 4.]

Finally, we conclude that

[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to 2^-} \dfrac {\vert x^2 - 4 \vert} {x - 2} = -4.]

Item 12 — Example: Evaluating a Limit Containing a Quadratic Absolute Value Function

Example Prompt:
Determine [MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to 2^-} \dfrac {\vert x^2 - 4 \vert} {x - 2}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, let's attempt to evaluate this limit by direct substitution. Substituting [MATH: x=2] into the limit, we obtain

[MATH: lim_(x → 2^{−})(|x^{2} − 4|)/(x − 2)|= (|2^{2} − 4|)/(2 − 2); = (|4 − 4|)/(2 − 2); = (0)/(0)]

which is an indeterminate form.

To evaluate the limit, we factor the numerator and rewrite the limit, as follows:

[MATH: \eqalign{
\lim_{x \to 2^-} \dfrac {\vert x^2 - 4 \vert} {x - 2}
&=\lim_{x \to 2^-} \dfrac {\vert (x+2)(x-2) \vert} {x - 2}\[5pt]
&=\lim_{x \to 2^-} \dfrac {\vert x+2\vert \cdot \vert x-2 \vert} {x - 2}\[5pt]

}]

Now, since [MATH: x<2,] we have

- [MATH: |x+2| = x+2] and
- [MATH: |x-2| = -(x-2).]

Substituting the above into our limit and simplifying, we get

[MATH: lim_(x → 2^{−})(|x + 2|⋅|x − 2|)/(x − 2)|= lim_(x → 2^{−})(− (x + 2)(x − 2))/(x − 2); = lim_(x → 2^{−})(− (x + 2)(x − 2))/(x − 2); = lim_(x → 2^{−}) − (x + 2); = − (2 + 2); = − 4.]

Finally, we conclude that

[MATH: \lim_\limits{x \to 2^-} \dfrac {\vert x^2 - 4 \vert} {x - 2} = -4.]
